body_text: BAT confirms Annie Goman to be appointed as new Managing Director of its corporate venture unit BTV. Annie takes over position from existing MD Juan Palacios, who is moving to new role within Reynolds American. Follows BTV announcement in December launching a new £200m fund to invest in wellbeing and stimulation. BAT has today confirmed the appointment of Annie Goman as the new Managing Director of its corporate venture unit Btomorrow Ventures (BTV). Annie joins BTV having previously held the role of BAT’s Global Head of Cannabis. Annie takes over the MD position from Juan M. Palacios, who is moving to a new role within BAT and returning with his family to the U.S. Juan’s new position as Senior Vice President of Business Development at Reynolds American, BAT’s U.S. subsidiary, will see him continue to partner with BTV as part of the Investment Committee, while working to find collaborations between BTV’s portfolio and U.S. operations. Annie Goman, BTV Managing Director said: “I’m very excited to be taking on the role of MD at BTV and to have the opportunity to work alongside our talented, dynamic teams at BTV and BAT, as well as within our portfolio companies. “I believe our approach to venturing and leveraging the capabilities of our minority investments plays a critical role in enabling BAT’s wider transformation and helping to build A Smokeless World. I look forward to continuing to strengthen these relationships as we deploy BTV’s Fund II.” Annie joined BAT in 2023, having previously held leadership roles within Commercial, Digital and eCommerce at ZX Ventures (the growth incubator arm of AB inBev), Innocent Drinks and Nestle. After graduating from Durham University, Annie built up a wealth of experience in the consumer goods space. At AB inBev, she successfully grew the eCommerce and DTC business from scratch at a country, European and global level. This involved partnering with the start-ups that were acquired by ZX Ventures and ensuring their seamless transition into ABI, making sure that the entrepreneurial and innovation mindsets were retained and embraced post-acquisition. Since its launch in 2019, BTV has made almost 30 investments in companies specialising in biotech & science; technology, and consumer brands across functional food and beverages. title: Best Tonneau Covers for the Honda Ridgeline: Complete Worksport Buying Guide
summary: A complete Worksport buying guide for Honda Ridgeline tonneau covers, including AL4, AL3, SC3, NEXUS, and SOLIS options with In-Bed Trunk compatibility.
body_text: Best Tonneau Covers for the Honda Ridgeline: Complete Worksport Buying Guide 🚛 Introduction The Honda Ridgeline is not quite like any other truck on the market. It is unibody, all-wheel drive standard, and comes with a feature no other production pickup offers: a waterproof In-Bed Trunk built directly into the bed floor. These quirks make the Ridgeline a uniquely capable lifestyle vehicle — and they also make tonneau cover shopping a slightly different experience than it is for any other truck in this guide. This guide covers every Worksport tonneau cover available for the 2017–2026 Honda Ridgeline, with direct attention to the question every Ridgeline owner asks first: "Will this cover block my In-Bed Trunk?" 🛻 The Honda Ridgeline: What Makes It Different The second-generation Ridgeline (2017–present) is built on Honda's unibody platform shared with the Pilot and Passport. Unlike conventional body-on-frame trucks — the F-150, Silverado, Tacoma, and every other truck in this series — the Ridgeline does not have a separate frame. This gives it a car-like ride, standard AWD, and a more maneuverable footprint, at the cost of towing capacity and off-road articulation relative to body-on-frame rivals. What the Ridgeline uniquely gains is the In-Bed Trunk (IBT) — a 7.3 cubic foot lockable, waterproof storage compartment accessed by lifting a section of the bed floor. The IBT is large enough for a spare tire, a full set of grocery bags, or gear you want completely concealed and protected from the elements. It is opened from within the bed, meaning the tailgate and bed floor surface above it must remain accessible. 📏 One Bed Size — No Configuration Choices The Ridgeline's bed measures approximately 5'4" (64") in physical length and is fixed across all trim levels and cab configurations — there is only one Ridgeline body style. In the Worksport vehicle selector, this bed is classified as a 5'0" bed. This is the simplest fitment situation in the entire Worksport buying guide series: you only need to confirm your model year, not your bed size or cab type. ✅ The Big Question: Do Worksport Covers Block the In-Bed Trunk? This is the first question every Ridgeline owner asks, and the answer across Worksport's lineup is generally positive. Because Worksport's covers clamp to the bed rail and fold toward the cab rather than using full-length sliding rails that run along the bed floor edge, they are designed not to interfere with the IBT lid operation. ✅ IBT COMPATIBILITY — CONFIRMED FOR AL3 AND AL4 Honda Ridgeline Owners Club forum users confirm that both the AL3 Pro and AL4 do not interfere with opening the In-Bed Trunk lid. The AL3 's rail system does not have a latch or clamp point between the second and third tri-fold sections that would block the IBT area. The AL4 , which opens as a single panel flipping toward the cab, clears the IBT lid when folded. Owners can access the IBT normally with either cover installed. For the SC3 and SC4 , IBT compatibility has not been independently confirmed via forum reports in current research — verify these via the live selector or Worksport support before publishing this claim for those covers. It is worth noting that the IBT lid opens upward from the bed floor, not from the tailgate end. Covers that clamp flush to the rail and fold toward the cab — like all Worksport designs — naturally leave the bed floor area unobstructed from underneath, which is why IBT compatibility is achievable across the lineup. A cover that used a crossbar system running the full bed width at regular intervals could potentially block the IBT lid; Worksport's panel designs avoid this. 💪 Worksport AL4 — Hard Flip-Up (Ridgeline) 🎬 Watch AL4 in Action The AL4 is Worksport's Made in USA hard flip-up aluminum cover — a single rigid panel that hinges at the cab end and swings fully upright, leaning against the rear window with the aid of gas struts. This gives you 100% unrestricted bed access without removing the cover. The AL4 's availability for the Honda Ridgeline was confirmed by community members in August 2025. Installation on the Ridgeline differs from conventional truck applications: the AL4 mounts directly to the tie-down cleat positions rather than using foam-sealed rail clamps. A Torx T-50 socket is needed to remove and reinstall the factory tie-down cleats during installation. No drilling is required. Make Model Years Bed Size Notes Honda Ridgeline (Gen 2) 2017–2026 5'0" Available for the second-generation Ridgeline (2017–2026) in the 5'0" bed. 🛡️ Worksport AL3 — Hard Tri-Fold (Ridgeline) The AL3 is Worksport's Made in USA hard tri-fold aluminum cover. Three rigid panels fold toward the cab in thirds, latching securely at each position. You can leave one panel unfolded for partial rear access, fold two for most of the bed, or stack all three behind the cab for full access. The Quick Latch mechanism at the tailgate end secures the cover with a satisfying click. The AL3 Pro is the most thoroughly documented Worksport cover for the Ridgeline. Honda Ridgeline Owners Club forum members have posted installation walkthroughs and long-term use reviews confirming it works well with the IBT lid and integrates cleanly with the Ridgeline's bed rail profile. A notable data point: one forum member who installed the AL3 on a 2025 Ridgeline reported that the box packaging was printed with a range of "2007 through 2022" — but they called Worksport directly and were told it fits the 2025 model correctly. This suggests Worksport may not have updated all packaging labels to reflect the extended year range. Always confirm your specific year via the live vehicle selector rather than relying on box labeling. Make Model Years Bed Size Notes Honda Ridgeline (Gen 2) 2017–2026 5'0" Available for the second-generation Ridgeline (2017–2026) in the 5'0" bed. The Ridgeline's unchanged bed profile since 2017 means the same part number covers the full year range. 🌟 Worksport SC4 — Soft Flip-Up (Ridgeline) The SC4 is Worksport's Designed in USA soft flip-up cover. Constructed from double-PVC coated, UV-protected vinyl over a lightweight aluminum sub-frame, the SC4 opens as a single panel — the same flip-up geometry as the AL4 , but in a softer, lighter-weight package. The SC4 is not currently offered for the Honda Ridgeline. Ridgeline owners seeking a soft cover should consider the SC3 . ⭐ Worksport SC3 — Soft Tri-Fold (Ridgeline) The SC3 is Worksport's Designed in USA soft tri-fold cover and the lowest-cost entry into the Worksport lineup. The tear-resistant vinyl tarp is UV-protected on both sides and sewn over lightweight aluminum cross bars. Three panels fold toward the cab, with snap-on fabric securing each section when folded. It is the quickest cover to install and remove in the entire lineup. Honda Ridgeline Owners Club forum members have posted reviews of the SC3 , generally noting it as a solid value option for the Ridgeline. The SC3 's installation uses the standard rail-and-clamp system on the bed top rail, leaving the bed floor — and the IBT lid — unobstructed. Make Model Years Bed Size Notes Honda Ridgeline (Gen 2) 2017–2025 5'0" Available for the second-generation Ridgeline (2017–2025) in the 5'0" bed. 🔥 Worksport NEXUS — Hard Folding Cover with Single-Side Uplatch (Ridgeline) The NEXUS is Worksport’s newest hard aluminum cover, launched April 2026. The proprietary Uplatch system auto-secures both bed rail sides from a single point of operation — you operate the cover from the driver side only, without walking around the truck. 16-gauge aluminum with DiamondSHIELD finish. Full bed access when panels fold toward the cab. MSRP $1,249–$1,349. Made in the USA. The Uplatch’s single-side operation is a particularly meaningful feature for Ridgeline owners. Because the In-Bed Trunk is accessed from within the bed, Ridgeline owners are already making more trips around the truck than owners of conventional pickups. NEXUS ’s single-side Uplatch means you secure or release the cover from the driver side only — minimizing the number of times you need to walk around the truck and making it easier to manage both the cover and the IBT in one stop. Make Model Years Bed Size Notes Honda Ridgeline 2017–2025 5’0” Single bed size ☀️ Worksport SOLIS — Solar Hard Folding Cover (Ridgeline) The SOLIS is Worksport’s integrated solar tonneau cover — a hard folding aluminum cover with embedded solar panels that charge your devices and accessories directly from the sun. For the Ridgeline’s 5’0” bed, the Small tier applies: up to 300W of solar output, priced at $1,999. SOLIS mounts to the bed rails and does not interfere with the Ridgeline’s In-Bed Trunk access, consistent with other Worksport hard covers confirmed for this platform. For full details and specifications, see the SOLIS buying GUIDE . Make Model Years Bed Size Notes Honda Ridgeline 2017–2026 5’0” Small tier — up to 300W / $1,999 📊 Quick Comparison: All Worksport Covers for the Ridgeline Cover Style Material Confirmed Years (5'0" bed) IBT Compatible? AL4 Flip-up hard Aluminum 2017–2026 Yes — forum confirmed AL3 Tri-fold hard Aluminum 2017–2026 Yes — forum confirmed NEXUS Hard fold — Uplatch 16-ga. aluminum 2017–2025 Yes — rail-mount (does not block IBT) SC4 Flip-up soft Vinyl Not currently offered N/A SC3 Tri-fold soft Vinyl 2017–2025 Yes — rail-mount design SOLIS Hard fold + solar Solar aluminum 2017–2026 Yes — mounts to rail, IBT unaffected 🎯 Which Worksport Cover Is Right for Your Ridgeline? 💪 Choose the AL4 if you want full bed access in one motion The flip-up design is the fastest way to open your entire bed — no folding in thirds, no stepping around panels. If you frequently load large or awkward items, the AL4 's full-panel flip gives you the most unobstructed access. The aluminum shell provides hard cover security and a premium look that complements the Ridgeline's refined exterior styling. The unique tie-down cleat mounting means installation is cleaner and simpler than on most trucks. 🛡️ Choose the AL3 if you want hard cover security with flexible partial access The AL3 is the most tested and community-documented Worksport cover for the Ridgeline. If you park outdoors, in exposed lots, or frequently carry cargo you want fully locked down, the AL3 's aluminum tri-fold panel with four locking quick-latches is the right call. You can also partially fold one or two panels to access a portion of the bed without opening everything. ⭐ Choose the SC3 if you want a soft cover at the lowest price The SC3 is a capable soft cover for Ridgeline owners who want weather protection and cargo concealment without the cost of aluminum. It is the lightest-weight option in the lineup and the easiest to roll back quickly. For a vehicle that often serves double duty as a daily commuter and weekend hauler, the SC3 is a practical, no-fuss choice. 🔧 Ridgeline-Specific Installation Tips The Ridgeline's bed rail profile and tie-down system differ from conventional body-on-frame trucks. A few things to know before you order: Tie-down cleats and the AL4: The AL4 on the Ridgeline mounts using the existing factory tie-down cleat positions rather than traditional foam rail clamps. You will need a Torx T-50 socket (not a standard hex or Phillips) to remove and reinstall the cleats. Plan for this before starting the install. Packaging labels: As noted in the AL3 section, Worksport's packaging may reflect an older year range. If your Ridgeline is a 2023 or newer, call Worksport directly at 1-888-554-8789 or confirm via the vehicle selector before assuming the cover will not fit. Platform continuity from 2017 through 2026 means fit is very likely, but the packaging may not say so. IBT access: All Worksport covers are installed on the top rail, not across the bed floor. The IBT lid opens vertically from beneath the cover's mounting plane, which is why the two are compatible. If you are using a non-Worksport cover with crossbar systems that span the full bed width at frequent intervals, measure carefully before assuming IBT access is maintained. ❓ Frequently Asked Questions Can I still open the In-Bed Trunk with a Worksport cover installed? Yes — at least for the AL3 and AL4 , where forum confirmation exists. Both covers mount to the top rail and fold away from the bed floor, leaving the IBT lid accessible from inside the bed. The SC3 and SC4 use the same rail-mount architecture and are expected to be compatible, but independent confirmation should be gathered before publishing this claim for those covers. The Ridgeline is not a 'real truck' — does it even need a tonneau cover? This is a common debate in Ridgeline circles. The Ridgeline's 5'4" bed may be shorter than most full-size trucks, but it is used actively by owners who haul gear, protect cargo from weather, and secure valuables. A tonneau cover is useful for the same reasons on a Ridgeline as it is on a Tacoma or Ranger — if anything, the In-Bed Trunk makes it more important to keep the rest of the bed weather-tight so the whole cargo system works together. Does Worksport make covers for the first-generation Ridgeline (2006–2014)? No confirmed Worksport fitment was found for the first-generation Ridgeline (2006–2014), which used a different bed profile and the original IBT design. All confirmed fitment in this guide is for the second-generation Ridgeline (2017–present). If you own a gen 1 Ridgeline, contact Worksport directly to ask whether any cover in their catalog is compatible. Will the AL3 or AL4 fit my 2025 or 2026 Ridgeline even though the box shows older years? Yes — both the AL3 and AL4 are confirmed for 2017–2026 via the Worksport live vehicle selector, so any current-production Ridgeline is in the covered range. Some older packaging labels may show a narrower year range; this reflects outdated print runs rather than actual fitment limits. The SC3 is confirmed through 2025. Always confirm your exact year via the live selector at worksport.com if in doubt. 🚀 Find the Right Worksport Cover for Your Ridgeline Use Worksport's interactive vehicle selector at worksport.com ( https://www.worksport.com ) — select Year → Make → Model → Bed Size and the tool will show every cover available for your Ridgeline's specific configuration. title: Gemini AI Security in Google Workspace: A Comprehensive Guide
summary: Secure Gemini AI in Google Workspace. Learn about comprehensive security features, best practices, and policies for confident, compliant AI adoption.
body_text: Introduction Google Workspace, enhanced by its integration with Gemini AI, is redefining productivity for organizations by streamlining workflows, boosting efficiency, and introducing intelligent automation. From drafting emails and summarizing documents to classifying data, Gemini empowers users with cutting-edge features while simultaneously raising the stakes for data security and privacy . This comprehensive guide is crafted for IT administrators, compliance officers, and security professionals seeking a clear understanding of the security features, policies, and best practices essential for the safe and responsible adoption of Gemini within Google Workspace. By leveraging these insights, organizations can confidently implement AI-driven tools while safeguarding sensitive information, respecting privacy, and meeting compliance standards. What is Gemini in Google Workspace? Gemini is an advanced artificial intelligence system that enhances various Google Workspace applications. Key features include: Email Drafting: Automatically generates responses and suggestions for emails, saving time and improving communication Summarization: Condenses large volumes of text into easily digestible summaries, streamlining information consumption Data Classification: Helps categorize and tag documents, improving document management and organization Unlike Bard – Google's standalone conversational AI – or traditional Google Workspace tools that primarily rely on direct user inputs and established templates, Gemini is deeply integrated within the Workspace ecosystem to deliver context-aware intelligence. While Bard offers open-ended responses and creative generation outside of core productivity apps, Gemini embeds its capabilities directly within Gmail, Docs, and Drive. This enables Gemini to provide tailored suggestions, automate repetitive processes, and classify data in real time, leveraging the contextual understanding of Workspace content and user permissions. As a result, Gemini bridges the divide between productivity and intelligent automation, making advanced AI features natively accessible to users without compromising on security or organizational control. Google's AI and Workspace Architecture A. Data Isolation and Access Controls One of the foundational principles of Google Workspace and Gemini AI security is the protection of user data. With this integration, data is isolated, and there are strict controls to ensure it does not become exposed to AI models. Gemini AI does not use customer data for model training by default, which prevents sensitive data from being inadvertently shared or exploited for further model development. B. Admin Controls and Permissions For organizations of all sizes, managing user access to AI-powered tools is critical. Google Workspace provides administrators with powerful role-based access control (RBAC), allowing them to assign permissions and limit who can access Gemini AI features. Additionally, admins can manage Gemini licenses and enable or disable specific features at the app level within the Admin Console, giving them full control over AI usage. C. Encryption Standards Google Workspace employs robust encryption standards to protect data both in transit and at rest: AES-256 encryption at rest and TLS encryption in transit ensure that data is kept secure at every stage of its lifecycle. Client-side encryption (CSE) is available for users who require an added layer of security, allowing them to encrypt data before it is uploaded to Google Cloud. D. Data Residency and Sovereignty For organizations with specific compliance or regulatory needs, Google offers data residency options to ensure that data is stored in the appropriate regions. Google Cloud offers flexibility, allowing users to choose the specific geographic locations where their data is stored, helping organizations meet local data sovereignty requirements. Gemini-Specific Privacy and Security Policies A. Prompt and Output Logging A key concern when using AI tools is whether interactions are logged for review. For Gemini, the following policies apply: Logs of prompts and outputs are maintained and accessible to admins to monitor the AI’s use, ensuring that no sensitive data is improperly handled. Admins can manage activity logs to track AI interactions and set retention policies, providing full transparency and the ability to review any activity that could pose security risks. B. AI Responsibility and Trust Principles Gemini adheres to Google’s AI safety protocols, which include: Red-teaming and bias mitigation strategies to ensure that AI responses are fair, unbiased, and aligned with best practices. AI watermarks and provenance features that enable traceability of AI-generated content, ensuring that its origin can always be verified. C. Compliance and Certifications Google Workspace and Gemini meet a wide array of global compliance standards, making it suitable for businesses in any industry, whether they’re in finance, healthcare, education, or beyond. Key certifications and frameworks include: ISO/IEC 27001, 27017, 27018 SOC 2/3, FedRAMP, GDPR, HIPAA Industry-specific standards and frameworks for sectors like education and finance Google’s commitment to compliance ensures that its solutions meet the stringent requirements of businesses and industries that must adhere to regulatory standards. Common Security Scenarios and How to Mitigate Risk As organizations adopt Gemini AI, it’s important to consider common security scenarios and take steps to mitigate potential risks. Some key considerations include: Preventing data leakage: Ensure that sensitive information is not inadvertently shared through AI-generated content by leveraging Data Loss Prevention (DLP) features. Avoiding prompt injections: Educate users about the risks of manipulating AI inputs and establish safe usage guidelines to minimize misuse. Managing Gemini in hybrid and BYOD environments: In flexible working environments, where employees may access Workspace from various devices, make sure appropriate security controls are in place to protect data integrity. Backup and recovery for business continuity: Implement robust backup and recovery strategies to ensure critical data can be restored quickly in the event of data loss, supporting ongoing operations and minimizing downtime. Admin Best Practices Checklist To maximize security and ensure responsible deployment of Google Workspace and Gemini , administrators should follow a comprehensive set of best practices. These not only safeguard sensitive information but also help maintain compliance and foster a culture of trust: 1. Review Access Levels and Permissions Regularly Conduct periodic audits of user roles and permissions to ensure only authorized personnel can access sensitive AI features and data. Remove unnecessary access promptly when employees change roles or leave the organization. 2. Utilize Context-Aware Access Policies Configure context-aware access to apply different security conditions based on user identity, location, device security status, and more. This helps restrict high-risk operations or sensitive data access when users are outside secured environments. 3. Enable Comprehensive Logging and Real-Time Alerts Turn on detailed logging for Gemini interactions and AI-related activities. Set up alerts to notify admins of unusual or suspicious behavior that could indicate data misuse or security incidents. 4. Ongoing Training and User Awareness Conduct regular security awareness sessions for staff to reinforce safe usage of Gemini and Google Workspace. Highlight real-world examples of prompt injection attacks and data leakage risks to build practical understanding. 5. Leverage Advanced Security Controls and Tools Implement VPC Service Controls to isolate sensitive resources and limit the risk of data exfiltration. Use DLP policies to automatically detect and protect sensitive data across all Workspace tools, including Gemini outputs. Apply encryption for both data at rest and in transit, and enable client-side encryption (CSE) where additional confidentiality is needed. 6. Establish Clear Retention and Archiving Policies Define retention schedules for AI-generated outputs and logs in accordance with your organization’s regulatory, legal, and compliance requirements. Ensure that archived data can be efficiently retrieved for audits or investigations. Gemini vs. Other AI Assistants When selecting an AI assistant for enterprise use, it’s important to assess security, compliance, and integration capabilities — core areas where Gemini stands out among its peers. Here’s a detailed comparison: Feature Gemini (Google) Microsoft Copilot ChatGPT Enterprise Integration Seamlessly embedded within Google Workspace; native integration with Gmail, Docs, Drive, and more. Deeply integrated with Microsoft 365 suite (Outlook, Teams, Word, etc.). Can be integrated via APIs and plugins; not natively embedded across productivity suites. Security & Data Protection Encryption in transit and at rest; supports client-side encryption; strict access controls and admin logging. Robust encryption and compliance features; leverages Microsoft security stack; granular admin controls. Enterprise version offers encryption, dedicated instances, and admin controls. Compliance Meets major standards (ISO/IEC 27001, SOC 2/3, GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP); audit trails for all AI interactions. Extensive compliance certifications (GDPR, HIPAA, ISO 27001, FedRAMP, etc.). Claims compliance with several standards; details may vary depending on deployment. Transparency & Control Admin visibility into prompts, outputs, and activity; configurable retention and DLP policies. Admin center provides control over data usage and retention; user activity monitoring tools. Offers some admin oversight, but levels of transparency and control may differ. AI Content Traceability AI watermarks and provenance features to verify source of generated content. Traceability depends on application; watermarking implemented in select tools. Limited watermarking; traceability features continue to evolve. Deployment Model Part of a closed, secure ecosystem, reducing risk of data sprawl. Closed environment, but interoperable with broader Microsoft security stack. Flexible deployment, but may expose organizations to more third-party risks. Ultimately, Gemini’s strengths lie in its native integration with Google’s secure environment, admin transparency, and extensive compliance. While Copilot and ChatGPT Enterprise bring their own advantages, organizations should carefully evaluate their unique risk profiles, regulatory needs, and existing tech stack when choosing an AI assistant. The Future of AI Security in Google Workspace The future of AI security in Google Workspace looks promising, with new features and advancements that will further strengthen data protection and privacy : AI-powered DLP tools that automatically classify and secure documents Adaptive trust models that adjust security measures based on real-time AI activity Upcoming features like “Gems,” which are AI-powered trusted agents designed to help automate and secure tasks within Workspace As AI technologies continue to evolve, Google remains committed to enhancing the security and privacy capabilities of Gemini AI, ensuring that organizations can adopt these innovations with confidence. When combined with Gemini, Google Workspace offers powerful AI capabilities while maintaining a strong focus on security . By leveraging robust encryption, compliance with global standards, and advanced admin controls, organizations can confidently deploy these tools while ensuring that their data is secure and compliant. Adopting the best practices outlined in this guide will help you maintain control over AI security, enabling you to harness the full potential of Google Workspace and Gemini without compromising your organization’s data integrity . Google Workspace and Gemini Security FAQs Is Gemini secure for regulated industries Yes, Gemini AI and Google Workspace meet numerous compliance standards such as GDPR, HIPAA, and FedRAMP, making them suitable for industries with strict regulatory requirements. Who can see my Gemini chats? Admins can access activity logs to review Gemini interactions. These logs are kept in accordance with retention policies to ensure transparency and accountability. Can Gemini outputs be archived for compliance? Yes, outputs generated by Gemini AI can be archived and managed in line with compliance regulations, ensuring organizations can meet legal and regulatory retention requirements. What happens if a user inputs sensitive data into Gemini? Sensitive data entered into Gemini is subject to Google’s comprehensive security measures, including encryption and DLP, to prevent unintended disclosures and maintain confidentiality. title: Why Your Gaming Username Is a Bigger Privacy Risk Than Your Password
summary: You’ve probably spent hours crafting a password that looks like a cat walking across your keyboard—uppercase, lowercase, symbols, the works. But your gamertag? That’s just a funny name you thought up in thirty seconds. And you’ve used it everywhere. Steam, Xbox, Discord, maybe even that old forum from 2012. The uncomfortable truth is that a reused gaming handle can unravel your entire digital life faster than a weak password ever could. Even more striking, 80% of internet users also game online, meaning most netizens carry a gaming profile packed with linkable data (OSINT Industries, 2026). Let’s pull back the curtain on why your username is the real skeleton key—and what you can do to fix it.
body_text: Why Your Gaming Username Is a Bigger Privacy Risk Than Your Password You’ve probably spent hours crafting a password that looks like a cat walking across your keyboard—uppercase, lowercase, symbols, the works. But your gamertag? That’s just a funny name you thought up in thirty seconds. And you’ve used it everywhere. Steam, Xbox, Discord, maybe even that old forum from 2012. The uncomfortable truth is that a reused gaming handle can unravel your entire digital life faster than a weak password ever could. With over 3.32 billion people actively playing video games worldwide, an enormous chunk of the internet is walking around with an OSINT‑friendly alias they’ve never thought to protect (Exploding Topics). Even more striking, 80% of internet users also game online, meaning most netizens carry a gaming profile packed with linkable data (OSINT Industries, 2026). Let’s pull back the curtain on why your username is the real skeleton key—and what you can do to fix it. The Identity Goldmine in a Simple Gamertag A gamertag is never just a name. It’s a persistent cross‑platform identity that, once someone knows it, can be used to uncover connected accounts, social media profiles, Discord servers, in‑game behavior patterns, and data breach leaks tied to that exact string (OSINT Industries, 2026). Tools like the open‑source Sherlock project can hunt for a username across 400+ social and gaming networks in seconds, instantly mapping everywhere that handle is registered (GitHub). A single tag like “xXDarkKnight2012Xx” might show up on Steam, Xbox, PlayStation, Minecraft, Discord, Reddit, Twitch, and a dozen YouTube gaming channels—all linked by that one string. And the publicly visible data is startlingly rich. By default, Steam profiles expose your game library, playtime, achievements, and friends list. Xbox hands out your gamerscore, recent games, and achievements. PlayStation reveals your trophy level and recently played games—all searchable by username alone (DigitalFootprintCheck, 2025). Just these breadcrumbs paint a detailed picture of your habits, your active hours, and the communities you orbit. What’s worse, changing your display name doesn’t reset the clock. Steam’s permanent 17‑digit SteamID64 never changes, and sites like SteamDB log every alias switch, preserving a full history you can’t scrub (DigitalFootprintCheck, 2025). On the Minecraft side, NameMC reveals a player’s complete username history, permanent UUID, skin and cape changes over time, and server history—all from one lookup. The bottom line: your gamertag isn’t a throwaway mask; it’s a permanent thread that, once pulled, unravels years of your digital history. How Your Gaming Username Opens the Door to Doxxing and Harassment Doxxing isn’t a niche hacker tactic anymore—it’s a mainstream public safety concern. Roughly 4% of U.S. adults (about 11.7 million Americans) have been doxxed, and 16% know a friend or family member who has been through it (SafeHome.org, 2026). Fear is widespread: 77% of Americans are at least somewhat worried about doxxing, with personal safety concerns climbing year over year. And yet most gamers cheerfully hand out the first puzzle piece for free. Doxxers thrive on correlation. They don’t need a single smoking gun; they chain tiny identifiers together. A gaming username appears in an old forum post, the forum profile links to a personal website, and suddenly a real identity is confirmed. Gaming platforms don’t make this harder—they integrate with Facebook, Twitter, Twitch, Discord, and YouTube, each connecting another OSINT door that can be pried open from one handle. The harassment stats underline just how exposed gamers already are. When nearly 78% of gamers report identity‑based harassment, threats, or offensive usernames, linking a gamertag to a real person is a recipe for real‑world danger. Your handle isn’t just a name—it’s the first domino that can topple into your home address, workplace, or family. The False Comfort of Changing Display Names Ask any gamer how they’d cover their tracks, and many will say, “I’ll just change my display name.” It’s a comforting thought, but it’s wrong. Beneath every shiny nickname sits an immutable account ID that third‑party databases have already recorded. SteamID64, Minecraft UUID, Xbox’s internal IDs—these are permanent and publicly referenced by tracking sites. NameMC doesn’t care that you’ve switched from “CoolDude123” to “ChillVibesOnly”—it keeps every past alias and presents them as a tidy timeline. SteamDB catalogues every display name change, so anyone with your profile URL can scroll through your naming history like a yearbook. And because most people reuse the same handle across multiple platforms, a fresh name on one service does nothing to sever the connections visible on another. Even deleting an account isn’t a clean break. OSINT tools and breach databases have already scraped the data. Cache layers, archives, and screenshots preserve the profile long after you’ve hit the delete button. Passwords can be rotated in sixty seconds; the underlying username IDs are forever. The Hacker’s Playbook: How Usernames Fuel Cyber Attacks Usernames aren’t just fodder for doxxers—they’re fuel for credential‑based attacks. Stolen credentials played a role in 31% of all data breaches over the past decade. And account takeover (ATO) attacks skyrocketed by 250% in 2024, even though 85% of targeted companies had bot detection in place. Gamers sit right in the crosshairs. Kaspersky detected attempted attacks using the names of popular Gen Z games to disguise malicious or unwanted files in the period April 2024–March 2025. The Hexon stealer campaign in November 2024 used fake game installers on Discord, Telegram, and MediaFire to vacuum up login data from Steam, Roblox, Minecraft, Epic Games, and Discord (Kaspersky). When a reused username gets caught in a breach, it becomes a skeleton key. Attackers check whether “ShadowHunter99” is the first half of an email address, try common passwords, and if the username contains a birth year—like “TexasGuy1990”—they have a narrow guess window for account recovery data (Avast). This is exactly where gamers and their data security habits fall alarmingly short: the disconnect between what players worry about and how they actually behave online is staggering. Why Passwords Get All the Love but Usernames Are the Real Weak Link The security world fixates on passwords—complexity, rotation, MFA—while usernames are treated like a non‑issue. But look at the numbers: 86% of gamers express concern about their personal data, yet data security ranks near the bottom of priorities when buying games. And trust is low: 83% think developers should safeguard their data, but fewer than 40% feel confident that current protections work. Here’s the harsh asymmetry: a password can be changed in minutes. A username, once leaked, is an indelible label that maps to multiple accounts across the web—a far juicier target for anyone running OSINT or credential‑stuffing campaigns. Hackers know this. They treat usernames as the index key that unlocks everything else, while ordinary users still assume usernames aren’t really “sensitive.” That assumption is the whole problem. Building a Separate Gaming Identity: A Practical Framework If your username is the root of so much trouble, the fix is refreshingly straightforward: stop reusing it. The golden rule of safe username creation is simple—never use the same username more than once, and never tie your gaming identity to your real name, location, or birth year. A powerful step is true compartmentalization. Privacy experts recommend building separate digital personas for personal life, professional identity, gaming communities, and anonymous browsing—each with its own email address, username, and profile photo, with zero cross‑contamination. On the practical side, you can generate a random, unlinkable handle for every gaming platform using a dedicated username generator . And don’t stop at usernames. Layer on a VPN to mask your IP and prevent network‑based tracking—this extra shield stumps DDoS attacks and keeps your real location hidden. This multi‑layered approach limits the blast radius: if one gaming account gets compromised, the attacker can’t pivot to your professional or personal accounts because there’s simply nothing to pivot to. Caveats & Counterpoints Not everyone needs a Bond‑villain level of operational security. If you’re a casual player who mostly hangs out in closed Discord servers with real‑life friends, rebuilding every identity from scratch might be overkill. Some platforms also make true anonymity hard—Discord’s blocking and privacy settings help, but social gaming is inherently about being seen. Conclusion Username hygiene is just one layer. Holistic digital privacy demands a broader shift in habits, but for most gamers, rethinking the humble gamertag is the lowest‑hanging fruit that’s been ignored for years. The goal isn’t to make you paranoid. It’s to replace the old assumption—that a username is harmless—with a clear‑eyed understanding of what that string actually carries. Your gamertag is a persistent, searchable thread that can connect your gaming life to your real identity in ways you never expected. Treat it with the same care you give your passwords, and you’ll be miles ahead of billions of other players who still think “it’s just a name.” Tags tech industry

title: Security Video Wall: What Makes It Effective
summary: A security video wall is only as effective as the intelligence behind it. See how AI-driven monitoring transforms static displays into adaptive command environments.
body_text: A security video wall is the coordinated display environment inside a security operations center that presents live and recorded camera feeds, alarms, and situational data to operators responsible for protecting people, assets, and facilities. For decades, the measure of a capable SOC was the sheer size of that wall. More screens signaled more coverage. That assumption is now falling apart, and the way leading teams design and operate these environments looks fundamentally different from what came before. Key Takeaways The showcase SOC is ending. Human attention degrades quickly during sustained monitoring, and real deployments routinely push operators far past those limits, making screen count a poor proxy for coverage. The video wall is becoming an inference layer. AI surfaces exceptions and humans make decisions, with incident-based dynamic layouts now standard in modern SOC and GSOC integration. Hardware, deployment, and design have all advanced. Direct View LED, software-defined walls on commodity servers, virtual GSOC models, and ergonomic standards define the current baseline. No amount of display quality solves the scale problem alone. Effective video wall planning requires an AI smart monitoring layer that curates feeds by activity, understands context, and detects behavioral precursors before incidents escalate. Why the Traditional Security Video Wall Model Is Ending The most consequential shift in physical security operations is the decline of the static monitoring wall. The Security Industry Association put it directly: the era of the "showcase" SOC, characterized by massive video walls and rows of operators watching screens, is rapidly drawing to a close . The reason is rooted in scale, not in operator effort. Human attention on video monitors degrades significantly after approximately 20 minutes , regardless of operator skill or training. Security professionals are skilled, but there are too many feeds for any single person to absorb simultaneously, regardless of dedication or training. These conditions describe a design constraint. Large walls can create more live video than any operator can absorb at once, especially when every feed is treated as equally important. A modern security video wall has to reduce the number of feeds demanding immediate attention, not simply enlarge the surface area available for display. Video Walls Become Inference Layers The defining trend now is the video wall's transition from a static repository for every camera feed into a dynamic inference layer that prioritizes and displays alert-driven content. The operating model has inverted: AI surfaces exceptions and humans make decisions. This means the wall no longer shows everything at once. It shows what matters, when it matters. Security teams increasingly prioritize systems that use AI to help operators navigate alarms and investigations, reduce noise, and elevate the events that matter. Incident-based layouts that automatically bring critical cameras forward are now standard in modern SOC and GSOC integration rather than a premium feature. Several AI capabilities are now shipping in production video wall deployments. Anomaly detection runs directly on the wall controller to flag unusual activity across live camera feeds. Machine learning learns operator workflow patterns and automatically arranges which cameras appear where. And alert summarization condenses noisy monitoring streams into a ranked set of tiles, so the most important events sit at the top of the wall instead of being buried in a grid. Unified Command Environments Improve Situational Awareness Security teams are moving away from fragmented multi-screen setups toward a shared command environment that delivers a real-time common operating picture . Instead of stitching together separate views for video, Physical Access Control Systems (PACS) , and sensor data across disconnected screens, operators now work from a single coordinated picture. This matters because threats do not respect system boundaries. Someone tailgating through a restricted east-side entrance and then moving toward sensitive equipment on the west side crosses multiple camera zones and multiple systems. A unified environment tracks that movement continuously rather than forcing operators to mentally reassemble disconnected views. During the seconds of reorientation that fragmented setups demand, situations escalate. Virtual GSOC Models Change Security Video Wall Planning The traditional on-site GSOC is shifting toward virtual, decentralized teams that operate remotely, delivering GSOC-level protection with comparable or lower total cost of ownership when all layers are counted. AI-driven automation increasingly replaces manual video monitoring, alarm prioritization, and dispatching, which reduces the need for large physical video walls and limits dependence on headcount growth. This shift is reinforced by economics. The VSaaS segment is growing quickly as organizations move more surveillance infrastructure into service-based and subscription models. The industry is also moving toward Hardware-as-a-Service and subscription monitoring models, where integrators manage hardware upkeep and analytics for recurring revenue. The staffing pressure behind this trend is real. More than 40% of security service providers named turnover as their top challenge, ranking it above margins and profitability, wage and labor compliance, accounts receivable, and insurance costs. High turnover and replacement costs make headcount-based monitoring difficult to scale, and teams cannot hire and retain fast enough to scale monitoring by adding people alone. Display Hardware Reaches a New Baseline The physical wall itself has advanced. Direct View LED is now the preferred choice for mission-critical environments, valued for long service life, close-viewing clarity, and bezel-free presentation. High-resolution display surfaces and flexible processing paths now define modern deployments, with future-proof design focused on clarity, reliability, and expansion capacity. A parallel shift is happening under the hood. A growing share of control room walls now run as software composited on commodity servers with standard GPUs, replacing proprietary hardware controllers. This software-defined approach delivers flexibility and lifecycle management advantages that fixed hardware controllers cannot match. Standards-Driven Ergonomic Design Shapes Security Video Walls Effective video wall design is increasingly measured against formal standards. The ISO ergonomic design standard for control centres provides the foundational framework for design principles, layout, workstation dimensions, displays and controls, environmental requirements, and evaluation. The SINTEF CCTV Human Factors Guidelines explicitly reference ISO 11064-1 as a compliance basis, while the RCMP's SOC Design Considerations Guide directs ergonomic design to follow ISO and other applicable guidelines and regulations. Concrete design requirements now guide serious deployments: Field of view and sightlines keep primary information in the operator's natural viewing area, with unobstructed sightlines from the console. Workstation space gives operators sufficient room for movement, collaboration, and adjustable equipment across different body dimensions. Environmental controls reduce distraction through low background noise and indirect, dimmable lighting that limits eye strain. Tiered data presentation is a recognized best practice for preventing cognitive overload: critical information sits front and center on the wall, while secondary data stays accessible but visually subordinate. Behavioral Detection Replaces Motion Triggers Legacy rule-based systems rely on pixel-based motion detection and simple triggers like tripwires and line crossings. They often generate excessive noise because they cannot interpret what activity means. Modern AI architectures interpret scenes contextually instead, understanding relationships between objects and distinguishing routine activity from genuine concern. The technology market has already moved beyond simple camera recording. AI detection technology is delivered through a mix of edge appliance, cloud, hybrid, and camera-side architectures, each with different tradeoffs for latency, bandwidth, privacy, and infrastructure cost. In every model, the planning question is the same: which intelligence layer determines what the wall should surface to operators? The operational payoff is practical. Visual cueing that automatically highlights relevant events helps operators focus on what requires judgment and response. Assistive computer vision is directly beneficial to detection accuracy because it reduces manual scanning and brings meaningful activity into view. Why Effective Security Video Wall Planning Requires AI Smart Monitoring The trends above converge on a single conclusion: a video wall is only as effective as the intelligence deciding what it displays. Buying larger, higher-resolution LED surfaces and arranging them according to ergonomic standards improves the viewing experience, but it does not solve the underlying scale problem. If the wall still gives every camera equal priority, operators still face more feeds than any person can absorb. AI smart monitoring is the layer that makes the modern video wall work. Rather than displaying all cameras in a static grid, the technology identifies which feeds show security-relevant activity and surfaces those automatically. Cameras covering routine areas stay processed in the background until activity patterns change. An empty loading dock during off-hours does not occupy premium display space, but when someone appears there outside operational hours, the system recognizes the deviation and elevates that feed. Recent advances in reasoning VLMs add contextual understanding to this monitoring. VLMs interpret scenes rather than simply flagging pixel changes, analyzing behavior and environmental patterns for a specific location and time. A forklift moving through a warehouse aisle during a shift reads as routine. That same forklift approaching a restricted server room overnight reads as an event that warrants attention. The system explains why activity matters, not just that motion occurred. This contextual layer is especially valuable for detecting behavioral precursors: loitering near a controlled entrance, a person falling, crowding, unauthorized access attempts, or someone running from a restricted area. Early warning on these indicators enables intervention before a situation escalates . When a threat is detected, relevant feeds and adjacent views surface automatically, tracking subjects across cameras so operators maintain visual contact without hunting through hundreds of feeds to find the right one. Ambient.ai and the AI-Native Security Video Wall Ambient.ai brings this model to life through Ambient Foundation , an AI-native platform where video management is a built-in capability rather than a separate system. For security teams, Foundation transforms the security video wall into an adaptive command view: Agentic Video Walls automatically surface the cameras that matter most in the moment, while Semantic Search lets operators find footage using everyday language instead of timeline scrubbing. The result is autonomous monitoring across every connected camera, freeing operators from manual feed scanning so they can focus on the events that require human judgment. To see how an adaptive, AI-native video wall performs in your environment, request a demo . Frequently Asked Questions How does AI-driven dynamic layout on a security video wall decide which camera feeds to prioritize and surface to operators in real time? AI-driven layouts analyze behavioral patterns, environmental context, and baseline deviations to prioritize feeds. The system evaluates object relationships, location norms, and time-of-day expectations, ranking feeds by security relevance. Alerts trigger automatic camera grouping with adjacent angles for situational context. What are the key differences between traditional rule-based motion detection and modern behavioral detection for security video walls, and how does contextual understanding reduce false alarms? Traditional systems trigger on pixel changes without understanding context, alerting on shadows or animals. Modern behavioral detection learns baseline activity and recognizes deviations, evaluating relationships between objects, location, and timing to suppress routine movements while escalating genuine threats. How do virtual GSOC models compare to traditional on-site security operations centers in terms of cost, staffing, and monitoring effectiveness? Virtual GSOC models eliminate fixed real estate costs and consolidate expertise across multiple sites simultaneously. Remote teams provide coverage flexibility across time zones, while centralized monitoring can reduce the need for dedicated operators at each site and limit proportional headcount growth.

body_text: Running a business across borders used to mean opening multiple bank accounts, waiting days for international payments and juggling expensive transfer fees. Today, business owners expect one platform that can receive payments, pay suppliers, manage team expenses and hold multiple currencies without unnecessary complexity. That's why digital business accounts have become increasingly popular with freelancers, startups and growing companies. Among the biggest names in this space is Revolut Business. Built for modern businesses, it combines multi-currency accounts, international transfers, expense management and accounting software integrations into a single platform. For many companies, it has become an attractive alternative to traditional business banking. But is Revolut Business the right fit for your company? The answer depends on how you get paid, where your customers are and which features you actually use. This guide explains Revolut Business fees, key features, limitations and the types of businesses that benefit most from the platform. What is Revolut Business and who is it for? Businesses no longer need separate banking tools for receiving payments, paying suppliers and managing multiple currencies. As more companies sell internationally, the demand has shifted towards digital platforms that simplify cross-border finance. Revolut Business was created to meet that need, giving businesses one place to manage global payments and day-to-day financial operations. Revolut Business is a digital financial platform designed for freelancers, small businesses, startups and larger companies. It allows businesses to hold, exchange and transfer money in more than 30 currencies, while sending payments to suppliers in over 150 countries. title: Follow the money: Inside the world of judgment enforcement and asset recovery
summary: In this video, Matt Toma explains how funded asset recovery helps businesses turn unpaid judgments and arbitration awards into real cash by combining capital with deep in-house enforcement expertise. Watch to learn more.
body_text: Matt Toma: Burford is the world's leading legal finance provider with unmatched expertise in asset recovery. Funded asset recovery is a solution that combines capital and expertise to help clients enforce court judgments and arbitration awards when debtors refuse to pay. There is no automatic payment mechanism in the legal system. Winning in court is sometimes only the beginning. Judgments remain unpaid because enforcement is costly and complicated as well as uncertain. Only 2% of in-house lawyers say they recover 100% of the value of their judgments and awards. Funded asset recovery transforms judgments into real income for businesses. Burford provides financing to cover enforcement costs, or we can purchase judgments and awards outright. When immediate liquidity is preferable to the carrying costs and risks of recovery in-house, purchasing judgments and awards outright can be a great option. Clients receive upfront capital that converts legal paper into cash. Unless we buy the judgment, the client remains in the driving seat. Unlike other funders, Burford has a deep tracing and enforcement expertise in-house, increasing our ability to assess cases and see them through. We have a deep track record of doing this kind of work all over the world, from common law jurisdictions to civil code countries onshore and offshore. We try to leverage the international networks that the debtors themselves have sought to exploit. So just because they're based in a country with a less than ideal legal system, it doesn't necessarily follow that their assets are. It's often the best option when assets are concealed overseas or hidden behind complex corporate structures. It's valuable when businesses lack the resources, time and expertise to manage enforcement effectively. Whether Burford funds, enforcement or purchases judgments, our capital is non-recourse, not debt or loan. We have an interest in recoveries only when and if the recovery succeeds. They gain access to enforcement specialists with extensive global experience. We combine scale, transparency and a proven track record of cross-border enforcement, and we offer flexible arrangements that adapt to the needs of each case. When clients fund their enforcement with Burford, they can be confident that they have the right partner in place to recover what they're owed.

title: How to Build REST APIs: A Beginner's Guide [2026]
summary: Learn how to build a REST API from scratch: what REST is, the HTTP methods and status codes to know, a step-by-step build, and the mistakes to avoid.
body_text: A REST API is where most beginners first feel the gap between following a tutorial and building something that holds up when a real request arrives. You can copy a working server line for line and still freeze the moment a request comes in malformed, or a route returns the wrong thing, or the database is empty. The syntax is rarely the hard part. The design decisions a tutorial skips are. Almost every app you use, on the web or on your phone, talks to a backend over a REST API. It is the seam where the frontend you can already build connects to data that lives on a server. Learning to build one is the bridge from frontend to fullstack, and it is more approachable than it looks once you separate the rules from the code. This guide covers what a REST API actually is, the rules that make an API RESTful, the HTTP methods and status codes you have to know, a step-by-step build of a working API, and the design and security mistakes that catch beginners. By the end you will know not just how to write the code, but how to decide what the code should do. What Is a REST API? A REST API is a web interface that lets programs exchange data over HTTP using standard methods, where each piece of data is a resource addressed by its own URL. More precisely, MDN defines REST (Representational State Transfer) as "a group of software architecture design constraints that bring about efficient, reliable and scalable distributed systems," where "a resource, e.g., a document, is transferred via well-recognized, language-agnostic, and reliably standardized client/server interactions." In plain terms: your data is organized into resources, and clients read or change those resources by sending HTTP requests to their URLs. REST is a style, not a protocol or a library. It was defined by Roy Fielding in his 2000 doctoral dissertation at UC Irvine, in the chapter titled "Representational State Transfer (REST)" . You do not install REST. You follow its conventions on top of HTTP, which is why a REST API written in Node looks recognizably similar to one written in Python or Go. A concrete example helps. Imagine a /users resource. A client sends GET /users to list users, POST /users to create one, and DELETE /users/42 to remove a specific user. Same resource, different actions, all expressed through HTTP. What Makes an API RESTful? An API is RESTful when it organizes data as resources with clear URLs, uses HTTP methods to express actions, returns standard status codes, and keeps each request stateless. Most of what "RESTful" means comes down to four rules. They are worth learning as a set, because breaking them is what makes an API confusing to use. The Four Rules of a RESTful API: Resources, not actions. URLs name things, not verbs. Use /users and /users/42 , not /getUsers or /deleteUser . The noun is the resource; the verb comes from the HTTP method. Methods carry the verb. Reading, creating, updating, and deleting are expressed through HTTP methods, not through the URL, following the HTTP request methods defined by MDN. Requests are stateless. Each request carries everything the server needs to handle it. The server does not remember the last request. This statelessness constraint comes straight from Fielding's REST definition and is what lets REST APIs scale across many servers. Status codes report the result. Every response carries a standard HTTP status code so the client knows what happened without parsing the body. One honest caveat: "RESTful" is a spectrum, not a pass/fail test. Plenty of widely used APIs bend a rule or two and are still perfectly good to work with. As a beginner, aim to follow these four consistently. That alone puts you ahead of a lot of production code. What HTTP Methods Do REST APIs Use? REST APIs map actions to HTTP methods: GET reads data, POST creates it, PUT and PATCH update it, and DELETE removes it. These five methods do almost all the work in a typical API. The table below pairs each one with what it does and the status code you would usually return on success. Method What it does Example request Typical success code GET Retrieves a resource or list of resources GET /tasks 200 OK POST Creates a new resource POST /tasks 201 Created PUT Replaces a resource entirely PUT /tasks/7 200 OK PATCH Updates part of a resource PATCH /tasks/7 200 OK DELETE Removes a resource DELETE /tasks/7 200 OK or 204 No Content The method definitions come from MDN : GET "requests a representation of the specified resource," POST "submits an entity to the specified resource, often causing a change in state," PUT "replaces all current representations of the target resource," PATCH "applies partial modifications," and DELETE "deletes the specified resource." One distinction matters in practice: idempotency . Sending GET , PUT , or DELETE twice has the same effect as sending it once, so a client can safely retry on a flaky connection. POST is not idempotent: send it twice and you may create two records. Knowing this saves you from a class of duplicate-data bugs later. What Do HTTP Status Codes Mean? HTTP status codes are three-digit numbers an API returns to tell the client what happened: roughly, 2xx means success, 4xx means the client made a mistake, and 5xx means the server did. MDN groups status codes into five families: informational (100-199), successful (200-299), redirection (300-399), client errors (400-499), and server errors (500-599). You do not need all of them. Five carry most of the weight for a beginner API: 200 OK - the request succeeded. 201 Created - a new resource was created, typically after a POST . 400 Bad Request - the server will not process the request because the client sent something invalid. 404 Not Found - the server cannot find the requested resource. 500 Internal Server Error - the server hit a problem it did not know how to handle. The fastest way to spot an amateur API is that it returns 200 for everything. When a failure comes back wearing a success code, the client has no way to tell what went wrong, and every consumer of your API has to guess. Returning the right code is not decoration. It is how the rest of the system, including code you did not write, reacts correctly to your responses. How Do You Build a REST API? To build a REST API, set up a Node.js project, define your resources and routes, handle each HTTP method, return JSON with the correct status code, then test every endpoint before you connect a database. Here is the path from empty folder to working API. The order matters more than any single line of code. Pick your stack. Node.js is a JavaScript runtime that lets you build servers in the same language you already use on the frontend, and Express is its most popular web framework for APIs. This combination is the common beginner path because it keeps you in one language front to back. Set up the project. Run npm init to create a project, install Express with npm install express , and create a single server file that starts listening on a port. Confirm it runs before you add any routes. Design the resources first. Decide your nouns and routes on paper before writing handlers: GET /tasks , POST /tasks , GET /tasks/:id , DELETE /tasks/:id . This is the step most tutorials skip, and it is the one that determines whether your API makes sense to anyone else. Implement the route handlers. Write one handler per method on each route. Each handler does its work, then sends back JSON and the right status code : 200 for a successful read, 201 after a create. Validate input and handle errors. Reject a malformed request body with a 400 rather than letting it crash the server. When a client asks for a resource that does not exist, return 404, not an empty 200. Add a data store. Start with an in-memory array so you can build and test the routes without a database in the way. Once the endpoints behave, swap the array for a real database and move your data into SQL. Test every endpoint. Use curl , a REST client, or just your browser for GET requests, and check each method against the status code you expect. An endpoint you have not called is an endpoint that does not work yet. If you build in this order, design first and database last, you spend your debugging time on logic you understand instead of fighting a database connection before the routes are even right. That sequencing is the difference between finishing and stalling, and it is the kind of read-run-fix loop that interactive courses, including Scrimba's, are built to drill into muscle memory. What Are the Most Common REST API Mistakes? A few mistakes show up again and again in beginner APIs, and each one is easy to avoid once you know to look for it. Verbs in the URL. /createUser instead of POST /users . The method already carries the verb. Wrong or lazy status codes. Returning 200 for created records, missing resources, and errors alike. Use 404 for not-found and 400 for bad input . No input validation. Trusting whatever the client sends, then crashing on the first surprise. Leaking internal errors. Sending a raw stack trace or database message to the client, which is both confusing and a security risk. No versioning. Changing an endpoint's shape and breaking every app that depended on it. A /v1/ prefix buys you room to evolve. No authentication. Leaving write endpoints open to anyone who finds the URL. That last point is the real line between a demo and a production API. An endpoint that anyone can call and change is fine on your laptop and dangerous on the internet. Security is not a step you bolt on at the end; it is a habit you build in from the first route. What Should You Learn to Build REST APIs Well? Building a REST API that survives real traffic depends on three things a tutorial cannot hand you: solid JavaScript underneath, a working sense of how the web moves data, and the security habits that keep an endpoint from leaking or breaking. None of those are learned by watching. They are learned by building, breaking, and fixing. That is the gap interactive practice is meant to close. Scrimba's scrim format lets you pause the instructor's screencast and edit their code directly in the browser, which is the same read-run-fix loop you just saw in the build steps above. The free Learn JavaScript course, taught by Per Borgen in partnership with Mozilla MDN, covers the functions, objects, the Fetch API, and async/await that every Node server is built on. It does not teach backend work, and that is the point: it gets the language out of the way so the server makes sense when you get there. Build your first API hands-on. The free Learn Node.js course, taught by Tom Chant, includes an 81-minute "Build a REST API" module that walks through exactly the kind of endpoints this guide describes. It is a focused introduction, not a deep dive into Express, databases, or auth, so treat it as the on-ramp. Go fullstack on the backend. For the data layer on its own, the free Learn SQL course pairs naturally with a REST API, and Learn Cybersecurity (Pro) builds the security instincts the mistakes section warned about. Node.js is worth the time regardless of where you learn it. It remains the most-used web technology among developers, reported by 48.7% of respondents in the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey , ahead of every framework and library. Frequently Asked Questions What is the difference between REST and an API? An API is any interface that lets two programs talk to each other. REST is one particular style of designing a web API, built on HTTP, resources, and status codes. So every REST API is an API, but plenty of APIs (GraphQL, gRPC, older SOAP services) are not REST. Do I need to know a backend language to build a REST API? You need a server-side runtime to run your API, but it does not have to be a new language. Node.js lets you build a REST API in JavaScript, the same language used on the frontend. What you do need first is genuine fluency in that language, especially asynchronous code. What is the best language to build a REST API? There is no single best language. Node.js with Express, Python with FastAPI or Django, Ruby on Rails, Go, and Java with Spring all build excellent REST APIs. For someone coming from frontend, Node is usually the smoothest path because it reuses the JavaScript you already know. Is REST still relevant in 2026? Yes. REST is still the default architecture for web APIs and is not going anywhere. GraphQL and gRPC have grown for specific use cases like flexible querying and high-performance internal services, but most public and internal web APIs you will encounter and build are still REST. Key Takeaways A REST API is a web interface for exchanging data over HTTP, where each piece of data is a resource addressed by its own URL. An API is RESTful when it follows four rules: resources not actions, HTTP methods carry the verb, requests are stateless, and status codes report the result. GET reads, POST creates, PUT and PATCH update, and DELETE removes; each maps to a standard HTTP method. Status codes communicate the outcome: 2xx for success, 4xx for client errors, 5xx for server errors. Returning 200 for everything hides failures. Design your resources and routes before you write handlers, and add a database only after the routes work. Building a REST API well rests on solid JavaScript, an understanding of how the web moves data, and security habits built in from the start.
